articles.title: What's the best place to get a personal loan?
articles.summary: Different types of lenders offer personal loans, but which is best? We discuss how borrowers can find the best place to get a personal loan.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

When you're looking for a personal loan, shopping around can help you get the lowest rate and best repayment terms. But what's the best place to get a personal loan?

Banks aren't your only choice. Though banks may be a good option for a personal loan, credit unions and online lenders are sometimes a better fit for your needs and preferences.

There's no one answer that works for every borrower — which lender is right for you depends on how much you want to borrow, when you need the cash, and your credit profile.

Many lenders offer unsecured personal loans — loans that don't require any form of property as collateral. The three major categories are traditional banks, credit unions, and online lenders, and each type of lender has its own perks and drawbacks.

Best for: Borrowers who need larger loan amounts

Many major banks, including Citibank, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, offer personal loans. While some lenders have relatively low loan maximums, such as $35,000 or less, major banks that operate brick-and-mortar locations tend to have high loan maximums and longer repayment term options. And, if you're an existing customer, you could receive your money faster.

However, some banks only offer loans to existing customers, and you must have a checking or savings account open for at least six months to qualify. And, personal loan rates from banks may have higher interest rates.

Best for: Borrowers who need smaller amounts or who have less-than-perfect credit

As nonprofit organizations, credit unions often offer their customers lower rates on personal loans than you can find from a bank. Plus, credit unions may have programs that make loans more accessible if you have poor credit or no credit. You may find second-chance or emergency loans that are lower-cost options compared to other bad-credit loans or payday loans.

The downside? Credit unions serve specific groups, such as those living in particular communities or employees of specific employers. That means you may not be eligible to become a member of a given credit union. These loans also tend to have lower borrowing amounts than loans from banks or online lenders.

Best for: Quick loan applications and disbursement

If you're in a bind and need a relatively large sum quickly, an online lender could be a good choice. These lenders often allow you to apply entirely online, and they can review and approve your application within minutes. If the lender approves your application, you can receive your loan funds quickly; some lenders offer same-day or next-day disbursement. That's a major asset if you have an emergency like a vet bill or a car repair you need to pay for ASAP.

There are online lenders that cater to different borrower types, including those with excellent or poor credit. To qualify for higher loan amounts and lower rates, you need very good to excellent credit.

How to choose the best place to get a personal loan

There are hundreds of lenders to choose from. When considering your loan options, these are a few key factors to keep in mind.

You want a lender that's responsive to questions, easily accessible when you have a problem, and has a solid reputation for handling customer issues. The J.D. Power Consumer Lending Customer Satisfaction Study is a great starting point. Look for a lender that scored above the segment average, as they are highly rated for the ease of their applications, digital platforms, and customer support.

It's also a good idea to look up lender reviews on sites like TrustPilot and the Better Business Bureau. These sites feature reviews from real customers, so you can get an idea of what it's like to take out a loan from that lender.

Some lenders cater to those with very good to excellent credit, while others have more relaxed eligibility criteria. Similarly, some lenders allow you to apply with a co-borrower or co-signer, but not all do. If you'll need a co-borrower due to a low credit score or insufficient income, look for a lender that permits it.

Consider how much you need to borrow, as loan amounts vary by lender type. With most lenders, you can borrow between $1,000 and $50,000. But lenders such as SoFi, Lightstream, and Alliant Credit Union offer personal loans up to $100,000.

For personal loans, the standard repayment options range from two to five years. However, you might be able to find extended repayment term options. For example, some lenders offer loan terms of seven or even 10 years.

A longer repayment term will give you a more affordable monthly payment, but you'll likely pay a higher interest rate and pay more in interest over the life of your loan.

As of June 2025, personal loan rates range from about 6.5% to 35.99%. The lowest rates are usually reserved for borrowers with excellent credit who choose a shorter repayment term, such as one to three years. For longer repayment terms or lower credit scores, expect a rate in the double digits.

While some lenders can take several days after approving a loan application to disburse loan funds, there are some — particularly online lenders — that boast loan disbursements as soon as the same day you apply.

Before you finalize a loan, make sure the lender is reputable. Banks and credit unions are both regulated by the FDIC and NCUA, respectively, and must adhere to certain rules and regulations. In addition, lenders must follow the federal Truth in Lending Act (TILA), which requires them to provide you with documentation about your loan, such as interest rate and repayment terms, before you're legally bound to pay it back.

Where things may get fuzzy is with some online lenders — those that aren't banks or aren't partnered with one. To make sure you're working with a legitimate online bank, avoid lenders that:

Offer guaranteed approval before you even apply

Require fees or payment before receiving the loan

Pressure you into applying or signing for a loan

Payday loans are short-term, high-interest loans that are, in general, due on your next payday. Payday loans tend to be small — around $500 or so — and are paid back through a post-dated check or by giving the lender authorization to debit your bank account on the agreed-upon due date.

But payday loans may be dangerous. They can carry high APRs of nearly 400% and may also come with excessive fees. In some states, payday lenders can roll over or renew a loan, charging fees to extend the due date past the next pay period, which can trap consumers in a cycle of debt.

Payday lenders, in general, don't look at your credit or personal finances when you apply for a loan. They only consider your income (since repayment is based on the lump sum of your next payday). And because it's common to need a payday loan when you're in a pinch — for example, if your car broke down or you have unexpected medical bills — it's easy for an unscrupulous lender to take advantage.

Some states prohibit or regulate payday loans, capping the maximum interest rate and fees you can be charged. Still, payday loans are rarely the best choice, even if you're strapped for cash, so it's best to pursue other options first.

What's a good interest rate for a personal loan?

Borrowers with excellent credit may qualify for personal loans with an annual percentage rate (APR) of about 7%. According to Federal Reserve data , the average APR for 24-month personal loans was 11.66% as of February 2025.

How do I qualify for the best personal loan rates?

The lowest personal loan rates typically go to borrowers with stable incomes and very good to excellent credit. If you don't meet that criteria, you may be able to secure a lower APR by adding a creditworthy co-borrower to your loan application.

Some lenders offer same-day loan disbursements, but typically, you can expect to receive loan funds within one to three business days after your loan paperwork is finalized.

Personal loans may have origination fees — a fee that covers the lender's administrative costs and is charged at the time of loan disbursement — and late fees if you miss a payment. Fees vary by lender, so carefully review the loan agreement to make sure you know all of the fees that you'll have to pay before signing.

How much can I borrow with a personal loan?

With most personal loans, you can borrow between $1,000 and $50,000, but there are some lenders with loan maximums of $100,000 or more.

How to compare personal loan offers: 7 crucial factors besides interest rates

A loan's APR is important, but so are fees, repayment terms, and customer service. This guide helps borrowers evaluate the full picture when choosing a lender.

How to get the best personal loan rate: 9 strategies to pay less for your debt

Your personal loan’s interest rate can have a major impact on your borrowing costs. Fortunately, you can take several steps to earn a lower rate. Here’s what to know.

7 personal loan myths that could cost you money

Don’t let common personal loan myths drain your wallet. Learn the truth about borrowing, interest rates, and repayment so you can avoid costly mistakes.

Best personal loans for bad credit for October 2026

Wondering if you can qualify for a personal loan with bad credit? It's possible. Here are some lenders to consider.

Too good to be true: How to spot personal loan scams

Not every loan offer is legit. Discover how to identify personal loan scams and keep your finances safe.

Here's what to know about average personal loan amounts and how to increase your borrowing power.

articles.title: Retirement planning: A step-by-step guide
articles.summary: Retirement planning can feel overwhelming. Find out how to save for retirement in this six-step guide.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Retirement planning involves estimating how much money you'll need when you retire and then developing a strategy for saving and investing your money. There's no magic number, but the goal is to have enough income to live the life you want after you stop working.

If you're not sure how to start planning — or if you have been contributing money to retirement accounts and want to make the most of your savings — you're in the right place. This step-by-step guide will provide a roadmap on how to save for retirement.

Step. 1: Budget 15% of your pre-tax salary for retirement savings

A good guideline is to save at least 15% of your pre-tax income in a tax-advantaged retirement account. If your employer matches a portion of your retirement contributions, that contribution counts toward the 15%. This percentage isn't etched in stone, however, and you may need to adjust your savings rate based on your situation and your goals.

Even if you can't save 15% initially, you can work your way up to that level over time. The important thing is to get started no matter how small the amount you can afford to save.

The IRS sets annual limits on how much you can contribute to retirement accounts. You can contribute more money, known as catch-up contributions, when you're 50 or older.

Don't worry if you can't afford to contribute the maximum amounts. Focus instead on what you can afford. What's more, aiming to save 15% isn't appropriate for everyone.

You're getting a late start on saving for retirement.

In either scenario, you may need to save more aggressively because you have less time to benefit from compounding. Compounding happens when your investment earnings generate more earnings. This process expedites your investment growth over time, creating more earnings potential the longer you stay invested.

When you have less time to save, your money has less time to compound, so you may need to save more to reach your retirement goals.

You have high-interest debt, like a credit card balance: Credit card interest rates are substantially higher than the returns you can earn from your investment accounts in an average year. Paying down credit card debt first may save you more money than you'd typically earn from investing returns.

You don't have an emergency fund: Try to build a three-month fund that you keep in a high-yield savings account . If you don't have emergency savings , you could be forced to withdraw retirement funds if you lose your job or get sick. That can be costly because, barring special circumstances, you will likely owe taxes and a 10% penalty on early withdrawals before the age of 59½. The long-term impact is even worse when you consider the lost compounding opportunity. Your money has less time to grow when you withdraw from investments early.

Here's a breakdown of your retirement account options.

The most common type of employer-sponsored retirement plan is the 401(k). However, if you work for the government or a nonprofit, you may have another type of retirement plan, like a 403(b) or a 457(b) plan.

Many employers match a portion of employee contributions to these retirement accounts. For example, your company may match 50% of your contributions up to 6% of your salary. In this scenario, you'd contribute at least 6% to get the full match. If you contribute 6%, your employer contributes 3%, bringing your total contribution rate to 9%.

If your employer matches some of your contributions, make it a priority to get the entire match. Otherwise, you're passing up free money.

An IRA is a retirement account that isn't tied to an employer. You can open an IRA regardless of whether you have a workplace plan. You'll need income from working (like a salary, hourly wages, tips, commissions, or self-employment income) during the tax year to contribute.

IRAs have virtually unlimited investment options and usually have lower fees than 401(k)s. If you don't have access to a workplace plan or your employer doesn't match contributions, an IRA can be a good way to start saving. The downside is that annual IRA contribution limits are much lower than 401(k) limits.

There are several retirement plans available for self-employed people, such as a Simplified Employee Pension (SEP), SIMPLE IRA, and Solo 401(k).

IRAs are available as traditional or Roth accounts. Many workplace retirement plans also offer these two options. The difference boils down to how you're taxed and eligibility.

Contributions to traditional 401(k)s and traditional IRAs are made with pre-tax dollars, meaning that the money you deposit in these accounts will often lower your taxes for the current year. However, you will owe taxes once you begin taking your distributions in retirement.

Contributions to Roth 401(k)s and Roth IRAs are made with after-tax dollars. There's no upfront tax break, but if you wait until you're 59½ and you've had the account for five years, your distributions will be tax-free.

Both traditional and Roth retirement accounts defer annual taxes on your investment income. This is different from a taxable account, which requires you to pay taxes on interest, dividends, and realized capital gains in the year they are earned.

Roth IRAs also give you the flexibility to withdraw all of your contributions (but not the earnings) at any time without paying taxes or a penalty. This is best avoided, though, unless you're facing a financial crisis. Note that income limits apply to Roth IRAs, so you may not be eligible to contribute if your earnings are high.

No. 3: Decide how to prioritize contributions to retirement accounts

Once you've selected your retirement accounts, you'll have to decide how to allocate your money. Here's a good way to prioritize:

Strive to contribute enough to get your employer's match on your 401(k) contributions.

If you have extra money to save, aim to max out a Roth IRA, if you meet the income requirements, or a traditional IRA. If you don't qualify for an employer-sponsored plan with a match, start with the Roth IRA.

After you've maxed out available IRA contributions, use extra money to make unmatched 401(k) contributions. You could also invest extra money in a brokerage account. Taxable accounts don't qualify for tax-deferred earnings, but they don't have withdrawal restrictions either.

Your contributions then need to be invested. Many employer plans have a relatively limited number of investment options, which are usually mutual funds. One easy option is to go with a target-date fund, which bases your investments on your estimated retirement date. IRAs have much broader investment access. Depending on the account, you may be able to invest in individual stocks, funds, bonds, and even real estate.

Many brokerages offer robo-adviser services, which use algorithms to decide how to invest the money in your IRA.

Social Security is another important part of your retirement plan. To see an estimate of your future retirement benefit and verify that Social Security's record of your earnings is accurate, create a Social Security account at ssa.gov.

While you're at it, brush up on the basic Social Security rules:

You're eligible for 100% of your benefit at full retirement age, which is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later.

You can claim retirement benefits as early as 62, but you'll receive a reduced benefit.

You can hold out for a larger benefit until age 70, at which point your benefit maxes out.

Your benefit is based on your 35 highest-earning years.

When you're beginning your career, you may not have much money to save for retirement. Focus on getting your employer's 401(k) match when you're starting out. But make it your goal to save more as your income increases or you pay down debt.

Budgeting for future financial milestones can help you achieve this step. Try layering in a bit more savings whenever your income increases or you cut an expense. For example, you could decide to allocate 25% of your next pay bump to your retirement accounts. Or, once you pay off your credit card or car loan, put the money that went toward monthly payments into your 401(k) or IRA.

No. 6: Work with a financial advisor, as needed

Once you've been saving for a while, working with a financial advisor may be worthwhile. A financial adviser can evaluate your investing activities to determine if you're on track to meet your goals. Advisors can also project different scenarios to show you how saving more, investing differently, or changing your retirement timeline may be appropriate.

Questions to ask while retirement planning

Consider the following questions as part of your retirement planning process:

How much money should I contribute to retirement accounts?

When should I take Social Security benefits?

If these questions feel hard to answer now, don't worry, they'll get easier as you go through the process of retirement planning.

In the early stages, your goals may be vague. You may only know that you want to stop working someday, but you're not sure how, where, or when. That's enough information to help you focus on setting aside savings and investing that money appropriately — and that's true no matter how much money you're able to save.

As retirement draws closer, you'll be in a better position to make specific plans, such as deciding where you want to live, when you'll quit working, and when you'll start receiving Social Security benefits.

Retirement planning is personal, and the amount of money you need will depend on the factors listed above, along with some things you have less control over, including your healthcare needs and how long you live.

So, how much do you need? An often-cited piece of conventional wisdom indicates that you should plan to replace up to 80% of your pre-retirement income once you've retired. Other estimates say 70% or less.

Fidelity advises people save between 55% and 80% of their pre-retirement income to maintain their lifestyle, but that percentage can be as low as 45% if you're "saving 15% each year from age 25 to 67."

Recommendations like these can provide an estimate for planning purposes, but the actual amount you need to retire is personal to you and depends on many factors, including your lifestyle and where you want to live after you stop working. For example, if you live frugally and retire debt-free, you'll need less money than if you plan to travel extensively or own multiple residences.

You can earn your targeted retirement income from different sources. Common options include:

Distributions from retirement accounts, including a 401(k) and individual retirement account (IRA)

Investment income from dividends or real estate

Your investing efforts in your working years can fund a 401(k), IRA, real estate purchases, or a taxable brokerage account. Depending on your age and risk tolerance, investments you might consider for your retirement and taxable accounts include:

Individual company stocks: You can usually hold these in IRAs and taxable brokerage accounts.

Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds or ETFs: 401(k)s, IRAs, and taxable brokerage accounts generally have access to a range of funds, each with its own investment strategy.

Target-date funds: Target-date funds own a mix of different investment types, like stocks and bonds. These funds adjust their holdings so that your risk declines as you approach your retirement date. They are meant to be held alone as the only asset in your portfolio.

Target-risk funds: Target-risk funds also have different types of assets, but they maintain a consistent risk level over time.

REITs: REITs, or real estate investment trusts, are companies that own and manage real estate. They earn on rents and property appreciation.

Your targeted retirement age is another important consideration. Retiring early may be the dream, but it can strain your finances. When you retire early, you have less time to save, and you need more money.

The sooner you start planning and saving, the better your odds of achieving a comfortable retirement. Remember, every dollar counts. Even if you can only save a few hundred dollars initially, that money will have time to grow and benefit you down the road thanks to the power of compounding.

Expect your retirement goals to evolve. Your plans will probably be vague when you're in your 20s and 30s. But over time, you'll get a better sense of what your retirement needs will be.

For many people, retirement planning is a multi-decade process of preparing for the day when they no longer get a paycheck from their job. The earlier you start thinking about and planning for retirement, the more likely you are to have built up enough savings to live comfortably after you stop working. Even if you're already in your 50s and can set aside only a small amount periodically, it's important to remember that even small amounts help.

How much do you really need to save for retirement?

Figuring out how much you need to save for retirement can be tough, especially if it's still a long way off. These guidelines can help you determine the right amount.

Retirement planning in your 20s: How to start saving for your future

Retirement planning in your 20s gives your money decades to grow. Learn how much to save, where to invest, and how to balance retirement with debt and other goals.

Retirement planning by age: The complete guide for your 20s-70s

Retirement planning looks different in your 20s, 40s, and 70s. See savings benchmarks by age and the retirement moves to consider in every decade.

Americans are feeling less confident about their retirement savings. Here are some of the best ways to get started early and set yourself up for retirement.

Retirement planning in your 30s means balancing saving with a growing list of financial goals. Learn how much to save, where to invest, and how to stay on track.

articles.title: PF ouve Vorcaro e Paulo Henrique Costa, ex-presidente do BRB, em inquérito sobre o Banco Master | G1
articles.standfirst: Costa foi ouvido pela manhã na Papudinha, e Vorcaro, no início da tarde na Papuda. Investigadores tentam esclarecer pontos como o aumento do capital do BRB e a tentativa de compra do Master.
articles.summary: Costa foi ouvido pela manhã na Papudinha, e Vorcaro, no início da tarde na Papuda. Investigadores tentam esclarecer pontos como o aumento do capital do BRB e a tentativa de compra do Master.
articles.body:
A Polícia Federal tomou nesta quinta-feira (15) novos depoimentos do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro e do ex-presidente do Banco de Brasília (BRB) Paulo Henrique Costa.

Os depoimentos foram tomados de forma presencial, em Brasília, onde os dois executivos estão presos – Vorcaro na Papuda, e Costa na Papudinha (prédio da Polícia Militar no mesmo complexo).

A TV Globo apurou que Paulo Henrique Costa foi ouvido ainda pela manhã. Já Vorcaro prestou depoimento durante a tarde, por cerca de quatro horas. O conteúdo das falas não tinha sido divulgado até a publicação deste texto.

➡️ O BRB – que tem como acionista majoritário o governo do Distrito Federal – enfrenta a maior crise de sua história, marcada por perdas bilionárias ligadas a operações com o Banco Master .

Os depoimentos foram tomados no âmbito do inquérito principal que apura as relações entre o Master e o BRB, entre 2024 e 2025.

➡️Em 2025, o BRB tentou comprar o Master e chegou a injetar R$ 16,7 bilhões no banco. A compra foi barrada pelo Banco Central e, depois, o BRB descobriu que parte das carteiras compradas era fraudulenta e sem lastro.

➡️A investigação também aponta que o ex-governador do Distrito Federal, Ibaneis Rocha (MDB), teve "atuação direta" na estratégia financeira do BRB que possibilitou a tentativa de compra do Banco Master, entre 2024 e 2025.

Daniel Vorcaro preso — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

articles.title: Petrobras bate recorde e chega a R$ 800 bilhões em valor de mercado; ações sobem até 110% em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: A estatal atingiu pela primeira vez a marca de R$ 800 bilhões na B3, após valorizar suas ações preferenciais em cerca de 100% e as ordinárias em 110% neste ano.
articles.summary: A estatal atingiu pela primeira vez a marca de R$ 800 bilhões na B3, após valorizar suas ações preferenciais em cerca de 100% e as ordinárias em 110% neste ano.
articles.body:
A Petrobras bateu recorde no valor de mercado ao atingir R$ 800 bilhões no encerramento do pregão na B3 nesta quarta-feira (14), a primeira vez que a companhia supera esse patamar.

Ao longo de 2026, as ações preferenciais da Petrobras ( PETR4 ) subiram cerca de 100% e as ações ordinárias ( PETR3 ) tiveram alta de aproximadamente 110%.

“Ao longo dos últimos meses, afirmei diversas vezes que quem apostasse contra a Petrobras iria perder dinheiro. [...] A companhia está forte, eficiente e cada vez mais capaz de gerar valor”, destaca Magda Chambriard, presidente da Petrobras.

🔎 Nesta quarta-feira, as ações preferenciais (PETR4) avançaram 2,22%, enquanto as ordinárias (PETR3) registraram alta de 1,94%.

Além do impulso trazido pelo cenário internacional de preços do petróleo, o mercado também reagiu a aos acordos de equalização de gastos e volumes referentes às jazidas compartilhadas de Berbigão e Sururu, na Bacia de Santos, assinados com as parceiras Shell, Total Energies e Petrogal.

Com o acordo, a Petrobras receberá cerca de US$ 859 milhões líquidos, a serem pagos até novembro de 2026.

A empresa também registrou uma produção própria de óleo no Brasil de 2,7 milhões de barris por dia no segundo trimestre, alta de 15% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025.

Também houve crescimento de mais de 10% da produção de combustíveis , em comparação ao segundo trimestre de 2025, com utilização recorde do parque de refino, que alcançou FUT superior a 100% no segundo trimestre do ano.

O recorde ocorre dias após a companhia ter superado pela primeira vez a marca de R$ 700 bilhões em valor de mercado (3).

Na ocasião, o movimento de alta foi impulsionado pelo anúncio de uma nova descoberta de petróleo em águas ultraprofundas, na Bacia da Foz do Amazonas , na Margem Equatorial brasileira.

articles.title: Brasil deve voltar ao top 8 das maiores economias do mundo em 2027, prevê FMI | G1
articles.standfirst: Projeções do Fundo Monetário Internacional indicam que o PIB brasileiro chegará a US$ 2,8 trilhões em 2027, superando Itália e Rússia; ranking considera o valor da economia em dólares, sem descontar a inflação.
articles.summary: Projeções do Fundo Monetário Internacional indicam que o PIB brasileiro chegará a US$ 2,8 trilhões em 2027, superando Itália e Rússia.
articles.body:
O Brasil deve voltar ao posto de oitava maior economia do mundo em 2027, ultrapassando a Itália e a Rússia, segundo as projeções do Fundo Monetário Internacional (FMI) em sua base de dados atualizada.

O Produto Interno Bruto ( PIB ) brasileiro deve alcançar US$ 2,796 trilhões no ano, ante US$ 2,772 trilhões da economia italiana e US$ 2,675 trilhões da russa.

🔎 O PIB é a soma dos bens e serviços produzidos por um país em determinado período. Os valores usados na comparação são nominais, ou seja, não descontam os efeitos da inflação, e estão expressos em dólares. Esse indicador permite comparar o tamanho das economias em uma mesma moeda.

Em 2026 , o Brasil ainda deve ocupar a décima posição, com PIB projetado em US$ 2,655 trilhões. A Rússia aparece à frente, com US$ 2,861 trilhões, seguida pela Itália, com US$ 2,702 trilhões.

A mudança prevista para 2027 ocorre porque o PIB brasileiro projetado supera o das duas economias europeias. O Brasil deve permanecer na oitava posição nos anos seguintes, segundo as estimativas apresentadas na base de dados, e alcançar US$ 3,398 trilhões em 2031.

Brasil deve superar US$ 3 trilhões em 2029

Além da mudança no ranking mundial, as projeções indicam que a economia brasileira deve ultrapassar a marca de US$ 3 trilhões em PIB nominal pela primeira vez em 2029 , quando o indicador deve chegar a US$ 3,056 trilhões.

Em 2026, o PIB nominal brasileiro projetado, de US$ 2,655 trilhões, também deve superar o maior valor anterior da série informada, registrado em 2011, quando alcançou US$ 2,614 trilhões.

FMI ainda vê desaceleração na economia real

Apesar do avanço previsto no ranking e dos valores nominais, o FMI projeta uma desaceleração do crescimento real da economia brasileira. A taxa deve passar de 2,3% em 2025 para 2,2% em 2026 e 1,9% em 2027.

🔎 O crescimento real mede a variação da produção de bens e serviços descontando o efeito da inflação.

A inflação brasileira, por sua vez, deve recuar gradualmente, de 5% em 2025 para 4,4% em 2026 e 4,1% em 2027. Já a taxa de desemprego projetada deve subir de 6% para 6,2% e 6,8% no mesmo período.

As projeções também apontam uma redução do déficit em transações correntes, indicador que mede o saldo das operações de bens, serviços, rendas e transferências entre o país e o exterior. O resultado negativo deve passar de 2,9% do PIB em 2025 para 2,4% em 2026 e 2% em 2027.

Logotipo do FMI é visto do lado de fora do prédio da sede em Washington — Foto: Yuri Gripas/Reuters

articles.title: TCU condiciona análise de contas do BC à conclusão da análise de liquidação do Banco Master | G1
articles.standfirst: Posição dos ministros segue recomendação do Ministério Público junto ao TCU (MPTCU) e contraria entendimento da área técnica do tribunal.
articles.summary: Posição dos ministros segue recomendação do Ministério Público junto ao TCU (MPTCU) e contraria entendimento da área técnica do tribunal.
articles.body:
A decisão foi tomada na sessão da 2ª Câmara do TCU, na última terça-feira (13), em uma análise em rea, ou seja, junto com outros processos e sem discussãoa atuação da autoridade monetária na liquidação extrajudicial do Banco Master.

Na prática, o TCU entendeu que as conclusões desse processo podem influenciar a análise das contas do BC e, por isso, decidiu aguardar uma decisão definitiva sobre o caso antes de concluir o julgamento das contas.

A posição dos ministros segue a recomendação do Ministério Público junto ao TCU (MPTCU) e contraria o entendimento da área técnica do tribunal.

O MPTCU recomendou suspender o julgamento do processo que analisa a liquidação do Banco Master, relatado pelo ministro Jhonatan de Jesus. Segundo o órgão, os fatos apurados nesse processo podem repercutir sobre o mérito das contas do Banco Central.

Já a área técnica havia proposto considerar regulares as contas dos responsáveis e conceder quitação plena, entendimento que acabou rejeitado pelos ministros. O relator das contas do BC é o ministro Jorge Oliveira.

A decisão foi tomada na sessão da 2ª Câmara do TCU, na última terça-feira (13), em uma análise em relação ou seja, junto com outros processos e sem discussão

O tensionamento entre o Banco Central e o TCU começou no fim do ano passado, quando o ministro Jhonatan de Jesus determinou que a autoridade monetária apresentasse, em 72 horas, esclarecimentos sobre supostos indícios de que a liquidação do Banco Master teria ocorrido de forma "precipitada". O ministro também decretou sigilo sobre o processo.

Dias depois, no auge do atrito entre os órgãos, Jhonatan determinou uma inspeção nos documentos do BC por considerar que ainda faltavam informações para embasar as explicações apresentadas pela autoridade monetária sobre a liquidação, decretada em novembro.

O Banco Central recorreu. Argumentou que a inspeção não poderia ser determinada individualmente pelo relator e deveria ser submetida ao colegiado do TCU.

Jhonatan acolheu o pedido para levar a discussão sobre a inspeção ao plenário, mas contestou o argumento apresentado pelo BC.

"Sob o ângulo regimental, não procede a premissa de que a inspeção dependeria, necessariamente, de autorização exclusiva de órgão colegiado", afirmou o ministro à época.

Jhonatan também disse que a decisão de submeter o assunto ao plenário levou em consideração a "dimensão pública" alcançada pelo caso.

Em meio a isso, um parecer da equipe técnica do TCU em fevereiro já afastava a existência de irregularidades ou omissões na atuação do Banco Central no processo de liquidação do Master.

"Concluiu-se, ao final, que não foram identificadas impropriedades, omissões ou negligência na atuação do Banco Central do Brasil . A decretação da liquidação extrajudicial foi considerada medida imperativa, legal e tecnicamente fundamentada, adotada tempestivamente após o esgotamento fático das alternativas de recuperação e diante da insolvência e da possível prática de ilícitos pela instituição supervisionada", diz o parecer dos técnicos envolvidos na auditoria.

Banco Master — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Em março, Jhonatan de Jesus suspendeu a análise da atuação do Banco Central na liquidação extrajudicial do Banco Master até a conclusão de outras investigações relacionadas ao caso.

Na ocasião, o ministro afirmou que aguardar os demais procedimentos permitiria ao tribunal decidir com um conjunto mais completo de informações.

“Entendo que a apreciação imediata do relatório de inspeção e do mérito da representação, neste momento processual, não se afigura a medida mais adequada, sob pena de o julgamento ocorrer com grau de completude inferior ao desejável, quando há perspectiva concreta de superveniência de elementos oficiais aptos a qualificar o juízo definitivo”, afirmou o ministro.

articles.title: TSMC stock drops despite record profit amid 'extremely robust demand' for AI chips
articles.summary: TSMC stock sank even after the company reported quarterly results that beat Wall Street estimates.
articles.body:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's ( TSM ) shares fell 2% despite strong quarterly results as a sector-wide sell-off weighed on the contract chipmaker.

TSMC reported a sixth straight quarter of record profits, with the company's bottom line jumping nearly 69% while revenue surged 51%.

The Taiwan-based contract chip manufacturer's sales are expected to reach as much as $54.3 billion for its current quarter, beating analyst estimates.

"Demand for our leading-edge technologies continue to be extremely robust," TSMC CEO C.C. Wei said during the call. "We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbot to AI assistance."

Third quarter gross margin was 66.4%, down from 67.7% in the second quarter. TSMC expects a gross margin of 65% to 67% for the fourth quarter.

"Given the continued robust multi-year demand from our customers, including the emerging agentic AI market, we reiterate our full-year 2026 capital budget to be between $60 billion and $64 billion," TSMC CFO Wendell Huang said.

The company expects capital expenditures from 2026 to 2028 "to be even more significantly higher than the past three years," as it continues to invest heavily to support customers' growth, Huang added.

The company is closely tied to the AI infrastructure build-out and its execution, as it manufactures advanced processors designed by chip giants such as Nvidia ( NVDA ), AMD ( AMD ), and Broadcom ( AVGO ).

TSMC stock is up more than 41% year to date as of Wednesday's close. Shares reached all-time highs earlier this month after Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk acknowledged early-stage talks with the world's largest chip foundry about a potential collaboration on his Terafab semiconductor initiative in Texas.

TSMC, which is already undergoing significant expansion in Arizona as part of a multiyear plan to manufacture chips stateside for its clients, confirmed it is exploring Texas.

"We send the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation," Wei said during the call. "We also talk to one of our customers who try to build a fab, Terafab, let me be more specific."

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: India’s current account deficit narrows to $5.2 billion in August, RBI data shows
articles.summary: India’s overall balance of payments (BoP) recorded a surplus of $45.4 billion in August 2026, compared with a deficit of $5.6 billion in the same month
articles.body: India’s overall balance of payments (BoP) recorded a surplus of $45.4 billion in August 2026, compared with a deficit of $5.6 billion in the same month last year, as foreign currency inflows, particularly non-resident Indian (NRI) deposits, rose sharply, according to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data.The overall BoP surplus also increased from $20.8 billion in July 2026, reflecting a sharp improvement in the country’s external financial position despite a continuing current account deficit.Banking capital inflows were a major contributor to the turnaround, reaching $64.7 billion in August, compared with an outflow of $4.7 billion in August 2025. Within this category, net NRI deposits surged to $83 billion during the month, against $1 billion in the corresponding period last year, the data showed.The increase in foreign currency inflows followed measures introduced by the RBI earlier this year to attract overseas funds and strengthen India’s external position.Current account deficit narrows in AugustIndia’s current account deficit narrowed to $5.2 billion in August from $6.1 billion a year earlier, even as the merchandise trade deficit remained substantial.The merchandise trade deficit stood at $26.6 billion during the month, compared with $27.6 billion in August 2025.Services trade continued to provide support, with the services surplus rising to $16.5 billion from $15.6 billion in the same month last year.Foreign direct investment (FDI) also improved, recording net inflows of $3.3 billion in August, compared with a net outflow of $0.1 billion a year earlier.Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) registered net inflows of $1.7 billion during the month, reversing net outflows of $2.6 billion recorded in August 2025.However, the cumulative figures for April-August showed continued pressure on the current account. The deficit widened to $18.3 billion during the five-month period, from $12.8 billion in the corresponding period last year.Despite this, India recorded an overall BoP surplus of $58 billion during April-August 2026, compared with a deficit of $0.8 billion a year earlier, according to the RBI data.RBI clarifies foreign exchange reserve requirementsSeparately, the RBI has clarified that its new Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR) requirements apply only to specified foreign exchange derivative contracts involving the purchase of foreign currency against the rupee.In a detailed set of frequently asked questions released on Thursday, the central bank said the reserve requirement would not apply to derivative contracts in which users sell foreign currency against the domestic currency.The RBI announced the regulatory measures, including the introduction of FERR, on October 10 against the backdrop of significant depreciation in the rupee. The domestic currency has strengthened against the US dollar since the announcement.FERR is a reserve that authorised dealers must maintain with the RBI for qualifying rupee-based foreign exchange derivative contracts. The requirement covers specified contracts undertaken by authorised dealers with users, as well as contracts used to hedge currency risks arising from their own assets and liabilities.The central bank said the requirement applies to specified derivative contracts between authorised dealers and users with a notional value exceeding the equivalent of $2 million."Accordingly, a derivative contract having a notional value of $2 million equivalent or less undertaken by an authorised dealer with a user is not subject to the requirement," the RBI said in its FAQs.The RBI defines a user as any person resident in India or outside the country, other than an authorised dealer.The central bank also cautioned authorised dealers against attempts to structure derivative transactions to avoid the provisions.The FERR clarification comes as the RBI seeks to regulate specified foreign exchange derivative exposures while its latest balance of payments figures show a sharp rise in overseas inflows during August.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anthropic Stands Alone as Rest of US IPO Market Slows to a Crawl
articles.summary: A cocktail of risks is threatening to stall the US IPO pipeline, leaving Anthropic PBC’s potential blockbuster debut as one of the few offerings that investo...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- A cocktail of risks is threatening to stall the US IPO pipeline, leaving Anthropic PBC's potential blockbuster debut as one of the few offerings that investors can count on.

Several deals have already come unglued, with smart-ring maker Oura Inc. and Bamboo Insurance Services Inc. postponing their plans as interest rates climbed higher and the Iran war dragged on. High-profile candidates SB Energy Inc. and Nscale Ltd. have filed publicly but haven't yet started formal marketing, further muddying the fourth quarter outlook.

Even with some deals falling by the wayside, equity capital markets bankers will be celebrating one of their best years ever for fees. Anthropic is seeking to match or exceed SpaceX's record-setting debut as soon as next month, in a listing that would dwarf all of the other potential deals combined.

Bankers concede that marketing IPOs has become much harder due to factors including the upcoming midterm elections, and investors are more choosy.

"This is the first time this year that there has been a bit of a pause in the IPO market where folks are saying, 'There's got to be a little bit of differentiation in terms of how we evaluate what we buy and at what price'," said Aloke Gupte, Citigroup Inc.'s co-head of global equity capital markets.

It doesn't help that the end-of-year calendar is trickier than normal due to the Nov. 3 midterm US elections, where AI safety and data centers have become part of policy debates.

"When you look at the US political landscape and geopolitics overall, the number of unknowns has gone up over the past six weeks alone," said David Bauer, JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s head of equity capital markets for North America. "That increase in uncertainty inevitably has an impact on how the market is going to behave."

A warning for the market sounded in September, with IPO activity slowing as US 10-year bond yields jumped more than 50 basis points. Only five sizable companies went public, raising $1.9 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, making it the slowest month since March.

That's in stark contrast with the picture for the year to date, bolstered by SpaceX and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix Inc.'s listings.
